name: S6 consequence
text:
If the second stage treats α̂ᵢ as data,
noise is mistaken for stable heterogeneity.
textPreview: If the second stage treats α̂ᵢ as data, | noise is mistaken for stable heterogeneity.

text:
Timing: ~1.25 minutes.
This decomposition assumes independent, mean-zero estimation error.
Sigma-squared denotes between-person variance; tau-squared-i denotes participant i's estimation variance, so the across-participant decomposition uses its average. With equal precision this reduces to sigma-squared plus tau-squared.
Tau-squared usually falls as the number and informativeness of trials increase, so the same population can appear more heterogeneous when participant estimates are weak.
Separate two-step fits cannot distinguish these two variance components without carrying estimate uncertainty forward.

[Sources]

This crop uses the first two rows of the original figure: response-bias population variance and between-session response-bias correlation. Columns are 80 and 640 trials.
Dashed lines are two-step; solid lines are hierarchical. Two-step variance is inflated and correlations are attenuated when local estimates are noisy.
Regression bias is not automatic: it requires estimation error related to the predictor. Classical outcome noise alone would mainly increase uncertainty.
This figure uses a broader subject-count grid, including S=500, than the shrinkage figure on the previous slide; treat them as separate simulations.

name: S13 EMC2 subset surface
text:
Participant-layer subset: design(list(v ~ x)) matches
the varying-coefficient structure of (1 + x | subject).
The likelihood is different.
textPreview: Participant-layer subset: design(list(v ~ x)) matches | the varying-coefficient structure of (1 + x | subject). | The likelihood is diffe...

text:
Timing: ~1.5 minutes.
This is a hierarchy crosswalk, not a brms lesson; the response likelihoods are different.
In brms/lme4, terms outside the bar are population terms and the subject-level bar explicitly selects which coefficients vary.
In EMC2, a subjects column is required but (1 | subject) is omitted: every free coefficient returned by design() gets a participant index.
Thus EMC2 v ~ x corresponds at the hierarchy level to a population intercept and x effect plus a participant-varying intercept and x slope.
Call this a constrained subset only at the participant hierarchy or linear-predictor level; EMC2 also uses specialized evidence-accumulation likelihoods.

[Sources]
- /Users/nstevenson/Documents/2025/EMC2_tutorial/Rfiles/Manning2022/analysis.Rmd, subject-level design section
- https://paulbuerkner.com/brms/reference/brmsformula.html

name: S14 formula takeaway surface
text:
Coefficients omitted from group_design() retain
an intercept-only mean and variance.
textPreview: Coefficients omitted from group_design() retain | an intercept-only mean and variance.

text:
Timing: ~1.5 minutes.
design() defines the local cognitive-model coefficients. Every free coefficient it returns has an alpha value for every participant; only known constants are excluded.
The displayed v_conditionB assumes treatment coding with level B. In actual code, every group_design() left-hand side must exactly match a name returned by sampled_pars(subject_design).
group_design() regresses the means of those existing alpha coefficients on person-level predictors. It does not create the participant effect.
If a coefficient is omitted from group_design(), EMC2 retains its hierarchical intercept and variance; it merely has no population predictor effect.
EMC2 can also include higher-level terms such as (1 | university) inside group_design(); the constraint described here is specifically the primary participant layer.
Sigma is the residual between-participant covariance matrix after the population regression.

[Sources]
- /Users/nstevenson/Documents/2025/EMC2_tutorial/Rfiles/Manning2022/analysis.Rmd, subject-level design and group design sections
- /Users/nstevenson/Documents/2025/EMC2_tutorial/Rfiles/analysis.R, group_design examples

name: S15 tradeoff surface
text:
TRADE-OFF
Fewer arbitrary crossed or multi-membership
structures than brms.
textPreview: TRADE-OFF | Fewer arbitrary crossed or multi-membership | structures than brms.

text:
Timing: ~1.25 minutes.
Participants are conditionally—not marginally—independent. They still borrow information because mu and Sigma are learned from everybody.
Conditional independence is not unique to EMC2. EMC2's advantage is that its participant-complete architecture preserves this partition and its specialized computation exploits it.
More general shared, crossed, or multi-membership structures are easier to express in brms/Stan but can prevent a pure participant-wise partition.

[Sources]
- /Users/nstevenson/Documents/2025/EMC2_tutorial/LatexFiles/main.tex, Factorized Hierarchical Model appendix
- https://paulbuerkner.com/brms/reference/brmsformula.html
